quote: a write whose cache line is already at hand can leave before an earlier write
problem: No earlier page defines 'cache line'. Chapter 1 only says a cache keeps a copy of the data and its neighbours (ch1-memory strip). So this reader cannot say what a write is waiting for, or why one write's line is at hand and another's is not, and that is the step this gloss uses to explain why writes leave out of order.
fix: name the line in the gloss: the block of neighbouring bytes a cache copies whole, which the core must fetch before a write to it can land
reason: Checked all five parts: 'cache line' first appears in ch16-lockfree-p3 and is defined only later, in ch16-numa-p1 (section 06). The gloss that explains why writes leave out of order rests on a term the reader has not met, and Chapter 1 never uses it. A one-clause gloss at first use is cheap and fits the book's habit of glossing in parentheses.
judge_fix: ch16-lockfree-p3, replace '... a write whose cache line is already at hand can leave before an earlier write still waiting for its line)' with '... a write whose cache line (the block of neighbouring bytes a cache copies as one unit) is already at hand can leave before an earlier write still waiting for its line)'. Optional: ch16-numa-p1 can then shorten its own gloss to 'cache line (the 64-byte block)' to avoid saying the same thing twice.

quote: the matching demand: everything the releaser promised is visible before any later load runs
problem: The paragraph explains only how writes get reordered, and release already guarantees that x is visible by the time the flag is. So this reader cannot say what would go wrong on the reading side without acquire. Nothing says the reading core can also run its load of x early, before its load of the flag (out-of-order execution from Chapter 1 applied to loads). 'Before any later load runs' hints at this but never says it.
fix: one clause: the reading core can also run its load of x ahead of its flag load, and acquire forbids that
reason: The paragraph explains only write reordering, and release already guarantees x is visible by the time the flag is. A reader cannot see why the reading side needs a tag. The reason is that the reader's core may run its load of x ahead of its load of the flag. 'Before any later load runs' hints at it but never says it. Fig 16.5's strip only says 'later reads wait', which does not say why. One clause fixes it.
judge_fix: ch16-lockfree-p3, replace '(the matching demand: everything the releaser promised is visible before any later load runs)' with '(the matching demand: no later load on this core, the load of `x` included, may run ahead of the flag load, so everything the releaser promised is visible by then)'.

problem: The step from the two shares to the formula is never given: count the one-core running time as 1, so the N-core time is (1 − p) + p/N, and speedup is the old time divided by the new one. Without it the reader cannot see why the formula starts with "1 /". p1's "90% parallel code" also points them at a share of the code, when p is a share of the running time (only Fig 16.8's drawn label says "time").
fix: one sentence before the formula: one-core time = 1, N-core time = (1 − p) + p/N, speedup = 1 divided by that time
reason: The callout gives the two shares (p4 explains the terms) but never says why the formula is 1 over the sum. That step is old time (1) divided by new time. Its How it works strip repeats the formula without it. The step is also what makes p a share of running time rather than of code. p1 says '90% parallel code', and only Fig 16.8's drawn label says 'time'. One sentence in p2 fixes both. The p1 wording should change too.
judge_fix: ch16-amdahl-p2, replace with: 'If a fraction _p_ of the one-core running time parallelises perfectly and the remaining _1−p_ is strictly sequential, count that running time as 1. On _N_ cores the sequential part still takes _1−p_ and the parallel part takes _p/N_, so the speedup (old time over new time) is:'. ch16-amdahl-p1: 'if a fraction _p_ of a program's running time is parallelisable' and 'a program that spends 90% of its time in parallelisable work maxes out at 10×'.

problem: From "the sequential portion stays constant while the parallel portion scales" the reader cannot reach N − (1 − p)(N − 1). The form that follows directly, (1 − p) + p·N (serial share done once, parallel share done on each of N cores), appears only in Fig 16.9's closed How it works strip.
fix: give (1 − p) + p·N in the prose with its one-line reading; keep the other form as "the same as"
reason: Verified the algebra: N − (1−p)(N−1) = (1−p) + p·N (N=64, p=0.95 gives 60.85, matching Fig 16.9's 60.9). The prose offers only the opaque form, and a newcomer cannot reach it from 'the sequential portion stays constant while the parallel portion scales'. The readable form exists only in a closed strip. Moving it into the prose, with its one-line reading, fixes this and also settles what 'speedup' measures here (finding 4).
judge_fix: ch16-amdahl-p7, replace 'and effective speedup, S(N) = N − (1 − p)·(N − 1), grows nearly linearly with cores.' with: 'so the work done in the same time, compared with one core, is S(N) = (1 − p) + p·N: the serial share is done once, the parallel share on each of the N cores. It grows nearly linearly with cores (the same as N − (1 − p)·(N − 1)).' Keep the closed strip as it is.

quote: the speedup is 5.9× on 8 cores, 15.4× on 64 and 19.6× on 1,024
problem: The drawn axis spaces 1, 32 and 1,024 evenly, so each step is a doubling, and neither the picture nor the caption says so. As drawn, the curve starts slow and is steepest in the middle, the opposite of the "rises fast at first" in the figure's description. reason: Viewed the 375 px frame and the SVG. The x axis has ticks 1, 32 and 1024 at equal spacing (x=46, 215, 384), so it is a log axis with no label saying so. The curve therefore reads as slow-start and S-shaped, and the desc's 'rises fast at first' does not match what is drawn. A reader checking the caption's 5.9 at 8 and 15.4 at 64 against the curve has to work out the axis. The finding's own fix is slightly wrong: each tick is x32 (five doublings), not one doubling. The defect is real, but the label must say that.
judge_fix: Fig 16.8 SVG, change the axis title 'cores, N' to 'cores, N (each tick 32 times the last)'. If that is too long at 375 px, use 'cores, N (log scale)'. In the figure's <desc>, replace 'rises fast at first and then flattens against its ceiling of 20' with 'climbs, then flattens against its ceiling of 20'. No change to the caption.

quote: and MESI's cache-line ping-pong
problem: The prose only ever presents MESI as the thing that keeps caches correct (p1, caption p3) and never says it costs time. quote: The stricter term comes from Maurice Herlihy's 1991 paper Wait-Free Synchronization, which proved a hierarchy of exactly which
problem: The paragraph credits Herlihy's 1991 paper with the origin of the term 'wait-free'. The term was already in print before that paper. Herlihy's own references include R. Newman-Wolfe, 'A protocol for wait-free, atomic, multi-reader shared variables' (PODC 1987). The 1991 TOPLAS paper is the journal version of Herlihy's 1988 PODC paper, and its introduction (p. 125) speaks of 'most recent work on wait-free synchronization'. So Herlihy did not coin the term. He made the idea precise and built the consensus hierarchy on it. 'Exactly which' also claims too much: the paper proves that an object cannot be built wait-free from objects on lower levels, and that some objects are universal. It does not settle every pair of objects. The §4r ledger row (Pass 18) checked only that the paper uses 'wait-free' (75 times) and never 'lock-free'. It did not check where the term started, so this finding does not reopen anything the ledger settled.
fix: Replace with: "Maurice Herlihy's 1991 paper _Wait-Free Synchronization_ (first presented in 1988) made the stricter notion precise and proved a hierarchy of which atomic primitives can build which data structures wait-free, turning an engineering practice into a mathematical theory." Source: Herlihy, ACM TOPLAS 13(1), Jan 1991, pp. 124–126 (footnote on the PODC Aug 1988 preliminary version; reference [23], Newman-Wolfe, PODC 1987), cs.brown.edu/~mph/Herlihy91/p124-herlihy.pdf
reason: Verified the claim overreaches: the term wait-free was in print before Herlihy (Newman-Wolfe PODC 1987 is cited in his own references; the TOPLAS paper is the journal version of his PODC 1988 paper). UNDER.md §4r only checked that the paper uses 'wait-free' (x75) and never 'lock-free', not where the term began. Herlihy made the notion precise and built the consensus hierarchy; 'exactly which' is also a bit strong. Real, small fix.
judge_fix: Replace the sentence in ch16-lockfree-p1 with: "*Maurice Herlihy*'s 1991 paper _Wait-Free Synchronization_ made the stricter idea precise, proving a hierarchy of which data structures can be implemented wait-free on which atomic primitives and turning an engineering practice into a mathematical theory." Update the §4r ledger row (now: 'made precise', not 'comes from'). Source: Herlihy, ACM TOPLAS 13(1), Jan 1991, pp. 124-149 (PODC 1988 preliminary version). Check the glossary entry for wait-free/lock-free and run npm run build:glossary only if the term cue text changed.

quote: A frame that must render in 16 ms, or one fixed compile, is Amdahl.
problem: Both p7 and this figure define Gustafson as the case where the time is fixed, and p7 gives 'more pixels in a rendering' as its example. A frame with a fixed 16 ms budget is the textbook case of fixed time: real-time graphics spends extra cores on more pixels and effects inside the same 16 ms, which is Gustafson. A careful reader sees the fixed time limit filed under Amdahl, contradicting the definition in the line above, and stops.
fix: "One fixed compile, or one query that must answer sooner, is Amdahl." (keep the Gustafson sentence that follows as it is)
reason: Internal contradiction. ch16-amdahl-p7 and the strip define Gustafson as 'fixes the time' and give 'more pixels in a rendering' as its example; the strip then files a 16 ms frame budget, which is a fixed time, under Amdahl. Real-time graphics spends extra cores on more detail inside the same 16 ms, which is Gustafson.
judge_fix: In Fig 16.9 strip 'Which applies', replace the first sentence with: "One fixed compile, or one query you want answered sooner, is Amdahl." Keep the Gustafson sentence as is.

quote: Six patients received radiation overdoses of up to a hundred times the prescribed dose; three died.
problem: 'Up to' makes a hundred times sound like the maximum, but the documented estimates go higher. At Tyler (first accident) the prescription was 180 rads and later simulations gave 16,500 to 25,000 rads, about 90 to 140 times. At Yakima the estimate was 8,000 to 10,000 rads against 86 prescribed, about 95 to 115 times. At Kennestone it was 15,000 to 20,000 rads against a typical 200. 'Roughly a hundred times' is the accurate summary.
fix: "Six patients received radiation overdoses of roughly a hundred times the prescribed dose; three died." Source: Leveson and Turner, 'An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents', IEEE Computer 26(7), 1993, pp. 23, 27–28
reason: Checked Leveson and Turner (MIT mirror of the paper). Tyler: prescribed 180 rads, simulations 16,500 to 25,000 rads (about 90 to 140 times). Kennestone: 15,000 to 20,000 rads against a typical 200. So 'up to a hundred times' understates the maximum; 'roughly' is accurate. Low severity, one-word repair.
judge_fix: "Six patients received radiation overdoses of roughly a hundred times the prescribed dose; three died." Source: Leveson and Turner, 'An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents', IEEE Computer 26(7), 1993.

quote: // the race: counter ends well short of 2,000,000, and differs from run to run
problem: This does not dispute the §4g range ('well short of two million'). It points out the condition the demo needs. With optimisation on, the compiler is allowed to assume no data race, so it folds each worker's loop into one add. I checked: clang -O1 and -O2 on x86-64 emit `addl $1000000, _counter(%rip)`, and on arm64 one ldr, add #1000000, str. Two threads then usually print exactly 2,000,000. On x86, even `++counter` on its own at -O1 compiles to one non-atomic `add [mem], 1`, not three instructions. A reader who builds the snippet with normal flags will not see the bug the comment promises.
fix: Change the two comments to: "// the race (built without optimisation): counter ends well short of 2,000,000, and differs from run to run" and "++counter;   // three steps: LOAD; ADD; STORE"
reason: Reproduced on this arm64 Mac with clang++ -std=c++17 and two threads of 1,000,000 ++counter each: -O0 gives 997602, 1020234, 1002354 (well short); -O1 and -O2 give exactly 2000000 on every run, because the compiler folds the loop (a data race is UB). A reader who builds the snippet with normal flags will not see the promised bug. Also 'three instructions' is not what an optimised build emits (one memory add on x86), while the prose and Fig 16.2 say 'three steps'.
judge_fix: In the ch16-races code block change the two comments to: "// the race (an unoptimised build shows it): counter ends well short of 2,000,000, and differs from run to run" and "++counter;                  // three steps: LOAD; ADD; STORE". Leave the rest of the block.

quote: Compare-and-swap · the atomic primitive everything else is built on
problem: The figure's own strip contradicts the title. On ARM before v8.1 (and on POWER and RISC-V), CAS is itself built from a load-exclusive/store-exclusive pair, so it is not the bottom layer. Atomic increments on x86 use `lock xadd`, not CAS. CAS is universal in theory (Herlihy), but saying everything 'is built on' it in practice claims too much.
fix: "Fig 16.4 · Compare-and-swap · the atomic primitive lock-free code is built on" (or "most other atomics are built on")
reason: The title says everything else is built on CAS, but the figure's own strip shows CAS itself being built from a load-exclusive/store-exclusive pair on ARM before v8.1, and x86 atomic increment is lock xadd, not CAS. The title is the most visible claim in the figure and overclaims; the section is about lock-free code, so scoping it there is exact and costs nothing.
judge_fix: Retitle (picture title, svg <title>, figure label, any index or a11y copy): "Fig 16.4 · Compare-and-swap · the atomic step lock-free code is built on". Strip and caption stay.

quote: the bug surfaces only on ARM or POWER
problem: RISC-V's memory model (RVWMO) also allows stores to be reordered with each other, so the same relaxed test can fail there. Naming only ARM and POWER leaves the reader thinking those are the only weakly ordered CPUs.
fix: "... and the bug surfaces only on weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM, POWER or RISC-V; ..." Source: RISC-V Unprivileged ISA spec, ch. 'RVWMO Memory Consistency Model'
reason: The strip says the bug 'surfaces only on ARM or POWER'. RISC-V (RVWMO) also allows store-store reordering, as do older weak machines, so 'only' is false and teaches that those two are the only weak CPUs. The picture label 'relaxed, on ARM or POWER' is an example, not an 'only', and can stay.
judge_fix: In Fig 16.5 strip 'Hardware differs': "x86 keeps stores in order, so this test passes there even with relaxed atomics, and the bug surfaces only on weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM, POWER or RISC-V; the compiler may reorder the two writes on any machine unless told not to."

problem: Code block comment '++counter; // three instructions: LOAD; ADD; STORE' (and p1 'nearly always well short'): on x86-64 the compiler usually emits one memory-destination add/inc. That is still a non-atomic read-modify-write, so three steps but not three instructions. At -O2, GCC and Clang may legally fold the whole non-atomic loop into one 'add 1000000' (a data race is undefined behaviour), so the demo often prints exactly 2,000,000. 'Well short, different every run' holds for unoptimised builds. 'Three steps' (the word Fig 16.2 uses) would be safe.
reason: Same defect as finding 4 (optimised build folds the loop; 'three instructions' vs 'three steps'), reproduced there. Apply once.
judge_fix: Same edit as finding 4; do not apply twice.

problem: ch16-lockfree-p1, 'The stricter term comes from Maurice Herlihy's 1991 paper': Herlihy already used 'wait-free' and gave the hierarchy in his PODC 1988 paper 'Impossibility and universality results for wait-free synchronization', and the idea goes back to Lamport's 1977 work on concurrent reading and writing. The ledger check (UNDER.md, 'wait-free' appears 75 times in the TOPLAS paper) shows the paper uses the term, not that the term started there. 'Made precise in' or 'formalised in' would be safer than 'comes from'.
reason: Same defect as finding 1 (the term predates Herlihy; 'comes from' overclaims; ledger check proved usage, not origin). Lamport 1977 is not a wait-free paper, so use only Herlihy's own prior-art facts for the fix.
judge_fix: Same edit as finding 1: "made the stricter idea precise" in place of "comes from"; apply once.

problem: ch16-gpu-p1: 'most of its scientific simulation' and 'most of the world's machine learning ... inference' are arguable as stated. Many simulation codes still run on CPU-only systems, even though the largest supercomputers use GPUs. A lot of inference runs on CPUs, phone neural chips and Google TPUs. 'Much of' would be safer, or the claim could be limited to the largest systems.
reason: Same class the ledger already corrected elsewhere (unverifiable 'most of the world's' claims, e.g. containers). Much simulation still runs on CPUs and much inference runs on CPUs, phone NPUs and Google TPUs (not GPUs). Training is the safe 'most'. Hedge the other two.
judge_fix: In ch16-gpu-p1 last sentence: "Today GPUs do most of the world's machine learning training and much of its inference and scientific simulation, and all of its real-time graphics."

problem: ch16-amdahl-p1: "a fraction p of a program is parallelisable" and "a program with 90% parallel code" are loose. In Amdahl's law p is the share of the one-core running time, not of the code. Figs 16.8 and 16.9 get this right ("time for one job: 5% serial", "5% of the time serial"), so the prose and the figures disagree on what p counts.
reason: Amdahl's p is the share of one-core running time, as Figs 16.8 and 16.9 say ('time for one job', '5% of the time serial'). Prose says 'fraction of a program' and '90% parallel code', which a reader can take as share of code, the one misreading that makes the law misapplied. Two-word repair, and the prose then agrees with the figures.
judge_fix: ch16-amdahl-p1: "...says that if a fraction _p_ of a program's running time is parallelisable, the sequential rest sets a hard ceiling on speedup that no number of cores can lift. The ceiling is brutal in practice: a program that spends 90% of its time in parallel work maxes out at 10×." Leave p2 to p4 as they are.

problem: Fig 16.8 How it works, "Other values": "going from 95% to 99% parallel buys more than any number of extra cores" holds for the ceilings (20× vs 100×), but not at small core counts. On 16 cores, 99% parallel gives 13.9×, below the 20× that 95% approaches with unlimited cores. It is true only once the machine has roughly 25 or more cores.
reason: Checked: 99% parallel on 16 cores gives 13.9×, and 95% parallel gets from 9.1× (16 cores) to 19.6× (1,024) by adding cores, so 'buys more than any number of extra cores' is false at small N. It is true only of the ceiling (20× vs 100×).
judge_fix: Fig 16.8 strip 'Other values': "50% parallel tops out at 2×, 90% at 10×, 99% at 100×: going from 95% to 99% parallel raises the ceiling from 20× to 100×, which no number of extra cores can do."

problem: Fig 16.8 picture vs its description: the <desc> says the curve "rises fast at first and then flattens", but on the drawn doubling axis it is S-shaped. A screen reader and a sighted reader get different shapes (see search point at ch16-amdahl-p6).
reason: Looked at the frame (fig-16-8-375-t7.333.png): the curve is plotted on a doubling axis (1, 32, 1024) and is clearly S-shaped, slow at the start, steepest near N=16 to 32, then flat. The <desc> says 'rises fast at first and then flattens', which misdescribes the drawing for a screen-reader user.
judge_fix: In the Fig 16.8 <desc> replace 'rises fast at first and then flattens against its ceiling of 20' with 'climbs steadily on the doubling axis and then flattens against its ceiling of 20'. Numbers unchanged.

problem: ch16-numa-p4: 'The fix needed updates to ... microcode and kernel page-table isolation' merges two different attacks. KPTI answers Meltdown. Microcode updates (IBRS/IBPB) and retpolines mitigate Spectre variant 2. Spectre variant 1 has no general fix, only barriers placed in the code one site at a time, and the Spectre class is still not fully closed. Read as written, 'the fix' suggests both attacks were simply fixed.
reason: 'The fix' reads as one complete fix, but KPTI answers Meltdown, microcode (IBRS/IBPB) and retpolines answer Spectre v2, and Spectre v1 has no general fix. One word is enough to stop the overclaim without adding expert detail.
judge_fix: ch16-numa-p4: "The mitigations needed updates to the processors' own internal code (microcode) and kernel page-table isolation (KPTI, which keeps the kernel's memory unmapped while a program runs, so every system call must switch page tables), and they left a lasting ~5–30% slowdown on syscall-heavy workloads."

problem: ch16-numa-p1: 'the 64-byte block' is stated as if every machine used it. It holds for x86 and most ARM cores, but Apple Silicon Macs (M1 and later, which the book names in ch1-cpu-p4) report 128-byte cache lines (sysctl hw.cachelinesize = 128). Not verified here. 'typically 64 bytes' would cover both.
reason: Verified locally: sysctl hw.cachelinesize reports 128 on this Apple Silicon Mac (Mac16,8), and the book names Apple chips in Ch1, so the owner's own machine contradicts 'the 64-byte block'. True for x86 and most ARM. Same number appears in the Fig 16.11 strip.
judge_fix: ch16-numa-p1 parenthesis: "(the block a cache stores and moves as one unit, usually 64 bytes)". Fig 16.11 strip 'Ping-pong': "...but share one cache line, that is **false sharing**; padding them apart fixes it."

quote: The trick: a speculative load used the secret to pick which memory location to touch
problem: This insight strip teaches the whole Spectre/Meltdown cache-timing mechanism again. Chapter 1 already taught it in ch1-cpu-p11, its caption ch1-cpu-p10 and the strip under it. The strip never points back, so it reads as new material, which breaks 'never explain twice what the book has already explained'.
fix: Replace the first two sentences with a back-reference: "*The cache as a side channel.* Chapter 1 showed how Spectre and Meltdown (January 2018) read a secret from the trace that thrown-away speculative work leaves in the cache." Keep the sentence about the fix and its cost (microcode, KPTI, ~5–30%).
reason: Ch1's insight strip (ch1-cpu-p11) already teaches the whole mechanism (speculative load picks one of 256 locations, cache keeps it, attacker times reads) and ends 'Chapter 16 returns to them'. The ch16 strip retells those steps instead of adding the cache angle, the KPTI fix and its cost.
judge_fix: Replace the first two sentences of ch16-numa-p4 (from 'In January 2018' to 'byte by byte') with: "In January 2018, Spectre and Meltdown (Chapter 1) turned the cache against itself: it keeps what thrown-away speculative work loaded, so timing reads of it leaks a secret across security boundaries." Keep the next sentence on the fix (microcode, KPTI, ~5–30%) unchanged, and keep the 'essentially every fast CPU since the mid-1990s' clause only if wanted (ch1 already says it).

quote: The classic example sounds harmless: two threads each increment a shared counter a million times.
problem: Chapter 4 §05 (ch4-ipc-p12) already taught the lost update (two processes read a count of 5, both write back 6) and the semaphore set to 1 that acts as a mutex. ch16-races-p1 and p3 teach both as if they were new. The brief asks for one clause naming the earlier idea instead of a second explanation.
fix: Open p1 with the link instead of its first sentence: "Chapter 4 showed two processes losing an addition on a shared count; threads share every variable, so the same race can strike any of them. The classic example: two threads each increment...". In p3: "The classic fix is the mutex (mutual exclusion lock), Chapter 4's one-at-a-time gate as a thread library object."
reason: ch4-ipc-p12 already taught the lost update on a shared count and the semaphore of 1 as a mutex. ch16-races-p1 and p3 present both as new with no pointer back. The ch16 treatment goes deeper (three steps, atomics), so keep it and add one clause naming the earlier idea.
judge_fix: p1: change the opening to "The price of shared memory is the lost addition of Chapter 4, now between threads: it shows up the first time two threads modify the same variable concurrently." p3: "The classic fix is a **mutex** (mutual exclusion lock; Chapter 4's semaphore set to 1 is one)."

quote: a write whose cache line is already at hand can leave before an earlier write still waiting for its line
problem: 'Cache line' is used here three sections before ch16-numa-p1 defines it ('the 64-byte block a cache stores and moves as one unit'). It appears nowhere earlier in the book, and the glossary dates its first use to ch16-numa. It also sits inside a parenthetical with an internal semicolon, while the subject 'Out-of-order execution ... and store buffers' waits a whole line for its verb 'let'. The sentence has to be read twice.
fix: "Out-of-order execution (Chapter 1, Section 04) and store buffers (holding areas where a core parks its writes until the cache takes them, which can let a later write out before an earlier one) let writes appear reordered."
reason: 'cache line' first appears in ch16-lockfree-p3, three sections before ch16-numa-p1 defines it, and appears in no earlier part. The parenthetical also holds a semicolon clause and separates the subject from its verb 'let'.
judge_fix: "Out-of-order execution (Chapter 1, Section 04) and store buffers (holding areas where a core parks its writes until the cache takes them, which can let a later write out before an earlier one) let writes appear reordered."

quote: a CUDA warp is 32 threads running in lockstep
problem: One unit of the GPU has three names. p1 calls it 'small cores', Fig 16.6 and its caption call it 'lanes', and p3 plus Fig 16.7's label call it 'threads' ('warp: 32 threads'). reason: The same unit is 'small cores' in p1, 'lanes' in Fig 16.6 and its caption and in Fig 16.7's code, and 'threads' in p3 and Fig 16.7's label. No sentence connects them. Combine with finding 28's p1 edit.
judge_fix: p1: "thousands of small cores (GPU makers call them lanes), grouped so that each group runs in lockstep on one instruction over different data." p3: "a CUDA warp is 32 threads, one per lane, running in lockstep."

quote: and MESI's cache-line ping-pong
problem: The chapter close lists 'cache-line ping-pong' as one of three constraints, but the term only appears in Fig 16.11's How it works strip, which is closed by default. No prose paragraph explains it.
